title: Raised by a single mother in Tulsa; the race riot and lost grandparents
summary: McBee describes his illiterate mother, her lost parents, and his belief that his grandparents died in the Tulsa riot, and starting a shoeshine box.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well I want to get back to that in a while because that sounds really uplifting. I wanted to make a few stops in your life that you had talked about two weeks ago, and first of all a brief question about your upbringing in Oklahoma. You said that the social conditions there were difficult when you were a child and I wonder if you could expand on that.

Well I was raised by my single parent mother. And there were three brothers and two sisters, right? I was number three in the rotation if you will. And I truly, you know, given recent news about Tulsa, Oklahoma, about conditions that took place during the race riots, okay? My mother had, all these years, had related to us that at eight years of age she had to drop out of school because of the loss of both parents in the same year. This was in © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

Southern Texas. And so she and her three sisters, elder sisters, she was the youngest of thirteen kids. They moved to Tulsa, and my mother, Alice, was the only one that had children which was of course us. And she — God I hate to say this — it’s very uncomfortable to say this but I never looked at my father in his eyes and said hello. Or who are you or what is this about. He was nowhere to be found. I think my older brothers, they knew him. They never talked about it. She never talked about it. And so she, when I would ask her about her parents she said, as I mentioned before, they passed away, you know, the same year. And that was it. You never really entered that conversation again. But now with the recent information about these Tulsa riots, you know, I think quite frankly she just didn’t want to disturb us because I think I lost my grandparents in that riot. And then, having moved to Tulsa when she was eight years of age so she said, she could not read nor write ‘til the day she died. So any information that she would impart to me about anything was rather limited. See? So the point is we as kids we had to make out on our own with, being young men, your first thought was to help her, to make sure the burden was off her, insofar as survival was concerned. You know it was always live — food etcetera etcetera. So I think my music began when, not that I realized that this could be my responsibility, that is, to take pressure off Mom, given my own individual needs. I built myself a shoeshine box, right? She gave me a couple of bucks and I bought some polish. I made a little piece of cotton material and a brush and I built this thing, right? You could put your foot on top of it and I would shine your shoes. So right to the right of our house were the railroad tracks. Right? A system of about eight tracks that, you know, provided, you know, travel between the west coast and the east coast. On the other side of that was the other side of town. And I built, I took that box, not knowing what the deal was, walked across those tracks and went into that area and started shining shoes. Right? Then I became pretty popular, this little kid. I was about nine or ten, right? Just nothing but cowboys, horses, and saloons. I remember hearing my first western music while I was shining some guy’s boots. And I got into that because it was like there was something rather tender about that music. You know it was usually somebody missing somebody or somebody feeling uncomfortable about something, the parting or whatever. And so I carried that with me for a while, until I began to grow up. I worked there as a salesman three or four years after that and, you know. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
